title: Learning from one stream
hookLine: each stream keeps some treasure well

lines: A RECIPE, A MAP, A HARMONIUM.
cards: A grandmother keeps the family's pickle recipe. An uncle remembers which villages the family came from. A cousin is the only one who still plays the harmonium properly.
Nobody holds everything. Lose one of them and something goes quiet in the family. The panth works a bit like that.
Over this block, stream after stream turned out to be guarding something particular. Today asks what each one keeps, and what anyone might borrow.

teach.b: Walk back through the streams and look for the treasure each keeps well. The Nihangs keep the old warrior dress, the martial art of gatka, and a playful, defiant way of speaking.

The taksals keep pronunciation: students learn to read Gurbani slowly, syllable by syllable, so that the Guru's words come out whole. The Nirmalas keep learning, scholars reading widely and explaining the Granth.

The Udasis keep a life of renunciation and care for shrines. The Namdharis keep simplicity, white dress, and kirtan sung in the old ragas. The gurmat sangeet schools keep those ragas alive for everyone.

Sikh Dharma sangats in the West keep early-morning practice, and some Western sangats explain things in English for newcomers. The rababis kept music at the Harmandir, and the dhadis keep history in the voice.
Not one of these is the whole panth. Each keeps a corner of the house well lit. Gurbani gives an image for this.

In Raag Suhi, around Ang 765, Guru Nanak speaks of a box of virtues: if someone has one, open it and enjoy its fragrance; and if a friend has virtues, become partners in them, and leave faults behind.
That's the posture of learning from a stream. You don't have to join it, or agree with it on everything.
You can borrow its fragrance: a slower way of reading, an earlier hour, a raga, a straighter back.
The streams lose nothing by sharing. That's how a fragrance works.

how: Some Sikhs learn from a stream other than their own: practicing gatka with Nihangs, learning pronunciation through taksal teaching, studying raga kirtan at gurmat sangeet schools, or joining early-morning programs in Western sangats.

games.q: what does “learning from one stream” mean?
o: joining a new stream and leaving your own behind
choosing the one stream that is most correct
borrowing one stream's strength without leaving yours

games.q: inside learning from one stream: tap the pairs.
p: open it and share the fragrance

s: to learn from a stream you have to join it
Guru Nanak's image is of sharing the fragrance of virtues, not changing houses.
taksal students learn Gurbani syllable by syllable
so that the Guru's words come out whole.
one stream holds the whole panth's treasures
each keeps a corner of the house well lit.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak, speaking of a friend who has virtues you lack. what do you suggest?
o: become partners in virtues, and leave faults behind.
ignore them and keep your own ways.
games.why: in Raag Suhi he speaks of opening the box of virtues and sharing its fragrance. learning from another stream works the same way.

practice: Go through the list once more, slowly, gatka, careful pronunciation, study, simplicity, ragas, the early morning, history in song, and notice where your attention lands.
Then make it small: read one line of Gurbani slowly, syllable by syllable, or listen to one shabad sung in its raga, and let it stay small.

wordCard.voice: Learning from one stream. Each stream of the panth keeps some treasure well, and anyone can borrow its fragrance without leaving their own. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: a school or lineage of teaching within the panth.

carryVoice: Your line: each keeps a treasure. A box of virtues, opened and shared. See you tomorrow.
